definition: Symbiotic means marked by a close, ongoing relationship between two different partners in which each one benefits from the continuing exchange.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word symbiotic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know symbiotic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The oxpecker birds and the zebras live in a symbiotic arrangement: the birds get a steady meal of ticks, and the zebras get rid of their pests.
Neighborly is weaker: neighborly parties get along and trade small courtesies, while symbiotic partners are bound in an ongoing exchange that both rely on.
Inseparable is stronger: symbiotic partners each benefit but might survive apart, while inseparable ones can no longer function without each other at all.

Interdependent means each side relies on the other to thrive, whatever the reason — trade, habit, need. Symbiotic began as biology's word for unlike species living in close partnership, and even used figuratively it keeps that flavor of two different kinds of partner locked in ongoing exchange.

Intertwined says two fortunes or histories are woven together so tightly they cannot easily be separated — it describes the tangling, not the payoff. Symbiotic makes the stronger, more specific claim that both partners actively benefit from a continuing exchange.

Win-win is the informal, business-casual way to say both sides come out ahead, usually about a single deal or arrangement. Symbiotic is the scientific register, and it describes an ongoing living partnership — a continuing exchange, not a one-time happy outcome.

Foresters once thought of the fungus threading through a pine's roots as a freeloader, stealing sugar from the tree.
Decades of soil studies overturned that picture completely.
The two organisms are symbiotic.
The pine sends sugar down to feed the fungus, and the fungal web hauls water and scarce minerals back to the pine from soil the roots could never reach alone.
Sever the partnership in a greenhouse and both sides suffer: the fungus starves within weeks, and the seedlings grow pale and stunted.
The exchange never closes: as long as both live, sugar flows one way and minerals the other, and each partner does better than it ever could alone.
